title: Open Datasets
text:
This page lists real, openly available datasets that are large and rich enough to support a full machine learning project. These are not teaching datasets. They are the actual data that psychologists publish on, which means you get real codebooks, real missingness, and real decisions to make.
A dataset worth building a project on usually has most of the following.
gss.norc.org | gssr package
Decades of United States survey data on social attitudes, happiness, religion, family, work, trust, political attitudes, social relationships, and demographics. You already met this dataset in the Feature Engineering unit.
The current gssr cumulative file packages the 1972 to 2024 GSS with 75,699 rows and 6,942 variables, plus several panel datasets.
Why it works. A very large set of candidate predictors, many possible continuous, ordinal, and categorical outcomes, real missingness and skip patterns, and an unusually good codebook. Different students can ask genuinely different questions from the same source.
Project questions. Predict self-reported happiness from social, economic, and attitudinal variables. Predict confidence in institutions. Predict social trust. Predict attitudes toward a social issue from broader values. Compare accuracy across historical periods.
gssr is not on CRAN, so it needs a non-standard install. Run this once in the console:
The author also publishes it through r-universe, if you prefer that route:
Then:
Caution. Do not throw all 7,000 variables blindly into a model. You need a substantively justified set of candidate features, and choosing it is part of the work.
openesmdata.org | R package docs
A curated collection of harmonized experience sampling datasets. Observations are collected repeatedly during daily life and typically include affect, stress, symptoms, context, and behavior. This is genuinely psychological data rather than generic tabular data.
Why it works. You can predict affect, stress, symptoms, or behavior at the next measurement. The repeated measures structure is an opportunity to see why ordinary random splitting can mislead you. It supports both person level and observation level questions, and the harmonization removes a lot of idiosyncratic preprocessing.
Run list_datasets() first so you can compare studies on sample size, number of time points, constructs, and design.
Project questions. Predict next observation affect from recent affect and context. Predict high stress moments from time of day and preceding states. Predict person average well-being from within person patterns. Compare person specific against population level prediction.
Caution, and this one matters. Do not randomly split individual rows into training and test sets when the same participants appear in both. Depending on your question, split by participant, by time, or both. This is one of the clearest real examples of leakage you will encounter.
cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes | nhanesA
Interviews, questionnaires, physical examinations, and laboratory measurements combined. Attractive for psychology because you can pair psychological variables with sleep, activity, medication, nutrition, and biological measures. The 2021 to 2023 cycle includes the PHQ-9 depression screener, sleep, physical activity, smoking, health status, and more.
Why it works. It mixes self report, behavioral, physical, and biological predictors, which makes feature engineering meaningful. It has realistic missing data and supports both classification and regression.
Project questions. Predict depression symptom severity from sleep, activity, and health variables. Predict self rated health. Predict sleep duration or sleep problems. Predict physical activity.
Caution. Watch for outcome leakage. Do not predict a PHQ-9 total score using the nine items that the total is computed from.
samhsa.gov
A large national survey covering mental health, substance use, treatment, functioning, and demographics for ages 12 and up. The public use files download directly in R format.
Why it works. Large sample, many binary and continuous outcomes, extensive codebook, and good material for logistic regression, regularization, trees, and calibration.
Project questions. Predict treatment utilization from symptoms and demographics. Predict broad categories of substance use. Predict psychological distress or functional impairment. Compare models across age groups.
Caution. These are sensitive outcomes. Frame your project as a statistical prediction exercise, never as a clinical or diagnostic tool. Also note that SAMHSA warns about trend comparability around the 2021 redesign, so pooling across years takes care.
cdc.gov/yrbs/data
High school student data on health behavior, sleep, activity, substance use, school experiences, and mental health. The 2023 national file has 20,103 usable records.
Why it works. Large enough for genuine three way splitting, with variables that are immediately understandable and many binary outcomes that make evaluation intuitive. The codebook is manageable compared with other federal surveys, and there are strong openings to discuss class imbalance and fairness.
Project questions. Predict insufficient sleep from school and behavioral variables. Predict physical activity level. Predict a school related behavioral outcome.
Caution. Participants are minors and some outcomes are sensitive. Interpret responsibly and do not present a class model as a screening tool.
cdc.gov/brfss
An enormous health survey. The 2024 file has 457,670 records and 345 variables, covering self rated health, mental health days, sleep, activity, disability, chronic conditions, and healthcare access.
Why it works. The sample size means you can hold out a real test set and compare simple against flexible models without running out of data. Good for rare outcomes and class imbalance.
Project questions. Predict number of poor mental health days. Predict self rated health. Predict insufficient sleep. Predict frequent mental distress.
Caution. With a sample this large, tiny improvements in a test metric become statistically detectable while remaining substantively meaningless. Do not confuse the two.
cdc.gov/nchs/nhis
A large annual health survey with separate adult and child public use files, released as CSV with extensive documentation. Depending on the year it covers psychological distress, functional limitations, sleep, pain, disability, healthcare access, and health behaviors.
Project questions. Predict self rated health. Predict psychological distress. Predict functional limitation. Predict healthcare use. Compare prediction across subgroups.
A good alternative to BRFSS when you want something a bit more focused.
midus.wisc.edu | Data access
One of the most psychologically rich large longitudinal datasets available. It was designed to study how psychological, social, and biological factors contribute to health and well-being across adulthood. The original sample was about 7,100 adults, with follow up waves and refresher cohorts.
Constructs include positive and negative affect, psychological well-being, personality, perceived control, stress, social support and strain, family, work, physical health, cognition, and biomarkers in some projects.
Why it works. You can build a psychologically meaningful model without assembling measures from a dozen unrelated sources.
Project questions. Predict later well-being from earlier psychosocial variables. Predict self rated health from personality, stress, and relationships. Predict change in an outcome. Compare demographic against psychological predictors.
Access. Public use through ICPSR or the MIDUS Portal, with registration and terms of use. Genomics, neuroimaging, and geographic files are restricted. Use the standard public survey files.
ICPSR public use archive
Follows participants from adolescence into adulthood. The public use archive spans 1994 to 2025 and does not require an ICPSR member affiliation. Strong on development, family, peers, school, mental health, health behavior, romantic relationships, education, and the transition to adulthood.
Project questions. Predict an adult outcome from adolescent characteristics. Predict educational attainment. Predict later self rated health from adolescent variables. Predict change across waves.
Caution. If you predict later outcomes from earlier waves, establish a clear temporal ordering first. Leakage here usually comes in through a variable measured after the thing you are predicting.
nlsinfo.org | Data access
Bureau of Labor Statistics longitudinal studies with extremely rich life course information, free through the NLS Investigator.
The full datasets contain over 100,000 variables, so build a custom extract rather than downloading everything.
Project questions. Predict college completion from adolescent characteristics. Predict employment or income category. Predict later health behavior. Predict family or work transitions.
Especially strong if you want a project about genuinely prospective prediction.
worldvaluessurvey.org
A major cross national survey of values and beliefs. Wave 7 contains more than 80,000 respondents across 64 societies, and the integrated EVS/WVS files are larger still. Covers life satisfaction, trust, social values, religion, family and gender attitudes, and political trust. Distributed directly as .rds and .RData.
Project questions. Predict life satisfaction. Predict generalized social trust. Train on one set of countries and test on another. Compare country specific against pooled models.
Caution. A random row split mixes respondents from the same countries across training and test. If your question is about cross cultural generalization, hold out whole countries instead.
ess.sikt.no | essurvey
A repeated cross national European survey with high quality measures of attitudes, well-being, trust, identity, inequality, and behavior.
The data portal also provides an API. You may need a free ESS account depending on the route you use.
Project questions. Predict life satisfaction. Predict generalized trust. Predict loneliness or social connectedness where available. Test generalization across countries.
Caution. Same as WVS. Country structure matters, and a random split answers a different question from a country holdout.
electionstudies.org
The core dataset for political psychology. The 2024 Time Series study has 5,521 respondents with pre and post election waves, and the cumulative file spans 1948 to 2024. Covers political identity, affect toward groups and candidates, trust, issue attitudes, participation, values, and economic perceptions.
Project questions. Predict turnout or participation. Predict political interest. Predict affect toward a candidate or group. Predict change between the pre and post election waves.
Distributed as CSV, SPSS, and Stata, all easy to import.
Project Implicit | Open data archive
Anonymized data from the Project Implicit demonstration website, including Implicit Association Test responses alongside explicit attitudes and demographics. Individual datasets can contain hundreds of thousands or millions of observations.
Why it works. A direct line to social cognition, at enormous scale, with a natural comparison between predicting implicit and explicit attitudes.
Project questions. Predict IAT D-score from demographics and explicit attitudes. Predict explicit attitudes from implicit measures. Compare performance across years, or train on one period and test on a later one.
Caution. The sample is self selected and not nationally representative. That is pedagogically useful as long as you clearly separate predictive performance within this sample from claims about the population. The files are also very large, so pick one IAT and one year to start.
openpsychometrics.org/_rawdata
Anonymous raw data from online personality and individual differences assessments. Most datasets are a ZIP containing a CSV plus a text codebook, which makes this the lowest friction option on the page.
Project questions. Predict a self reported personality category from item responses. Predict demographic or behavioral variables from personality items. Compare sparse regression against tree based models. Test whether a short subset of items predicts a longer scale score.
Caution. Volunteer internet samples, so discuss self selection explicitly. And avoid trivial targets, such as predicting a scale score from the exact items summed to create it, unless scale shortening is the actual point.
cps.ipums.org
Harmonized decades of monthly United States Current Population Survey microdata. Free after registration, and you build a custom extract rather than downloading everything. Covers employment, education, family structure, income, disability, health insurance, food security, and selected supplements on volunteering and internet use.
Project questions. Predict labor force participation. Predict food insecurity. Predict employment transitions. Predict volunteering.
Less purely psychological than MIDUS or openESM, but strong for social, occupational, and developmental questions.
hrs.isr.umich.edu
A major longitudinal study of United States adults over 50 and their spouses, available after registration. Covers cognition, depression, personality, health, disability, family, work and retirement, economic stress, and social engagement.
Project questions. Predict later cognitive performance. Predict retirement transition. Predict self rated health or functional limitation. Predict depressive symptoms from social, economic, and health variables.
An excellent advanced project, though access and longitudinal data management make it harder than GSS or NHANES.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Simple Linear Regression predicted second semester grade from a single predictor. This page adds more predictors. Adding predictors never makes the fit to the training data worse, so the question is whether the model predicts better.
library(dplyr)    # data manipulation and the pipe
library(ggplot2)  # plots
library(caret)    # train() for fitting and cross validation
library(rsample)  # splitting
library(vip)      # variable importance plots
We continue with the student dropout data from the previous page. If you did not build it there, download dropout.csv.
dropout <- read.csv("data/dropout.csv", sep = ";") %>%
  rename(
    grade_sem1      = Curricular.units.1st.sem..grade.,
    grade_sem2      = Curricular.units.2nd.sem..grade.,
    units_sem1      = Curricular.units.1st.sem..approved.,
    admission_grade = Admission.grade,
    prev_grade      = Previous.qualification..grade.,
    age             = Age.at.enrollment,
    scholarship     = Scholarship.holder,
    fees_current    = Tuition.fees.up.to.date
  )

# Same decision as the previous page: keep students who completed units,
# so the model is not just separating completers from non-completers
completers <- dropout %>% filter(grade_sem1 > 0, grade_sem2 > 0)

nrow(completers)

[1] 3512
Multiple linear regression extends the simple linear regression framework to include more than one predictor:
It models the relationship between a single outcome \(Y_i\) and multiple predictors \(X_{1i}, X_{2i}, \dots, X_{pi}\) for each observation \(i = 1, \dots, n\).
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \dots + \beta_p X_{pi} + \varepsilon_i
\]
where:
The coefficients are estimated by ordinary least squares, which chooses the values minimizing the residual sum of squares:
\[
\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
\]
This is the same loss function idea from the previous page. Nothing about the learning procedure changes when you add predictors. There are simply more coefficients to search over.
Predictors are joined with + on the right hand side of the formula.
fit_mlr <- lm(grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1 + admission_grade, data = completers)

coef(fit_mlr)

    (Intercept)      grade_sem1 admission_grade 
    3.220254141     0.674053933     0.007326894
Each \(\beta_j\) reflects the unique contribution of its predictor, after adjusting for the others.
b <- coef(fit_mlr)
Admission grade on its own is related to second semester grade, but much of what it tells you is already contained in the first semester grade. Its coefficient reports only what it adds.
An interaction occurs when the effect of one predictor depends on the level of another. In other words, one variable is moderated by another.
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \beta_3 (X_{1i} \cdot X_{2i}) + \varepsilon_i
\]
where \(\beta_3\) captures the interaction, and \((X_{1i} \cdot X_{2i})\) is the product of the two predictors. If \(\beta_3 \neq 0\), the effect of \(X_1\) on \(Y\) changes depending on \(X_2\).
Without an interaction, the model assumes each predictor contributes independently, which may oversimplify reality.
# The colon creates the product term
fit_interaction <- lm(
  grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1 + admission_grade + grade_sem1:admission_grade,
  data = completers
)

coef(fit_interaction)

               (Intercept)                 grade_sem1 
               6.701053190                0.405048615 
           admission_grade grade_sem1:admission_grade 
              -0.019620445                0.002074745
In this course the goal is prediction, so we return to the splitting and cross validation framework from the pipeline unit.
set.seed(123)

split <- initial_split(completers, prop = 0.7, strata = "grade_sem2")
train  <- training(split)
test   <- testing(split)

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))

train  test 
 2456  1056
# 10 fold cross validation, used identically for every model below so the
# comparison between them is fair
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)
We compare four models of increasing complexity.
set.seed(123)
cv_model1 <- train(grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1,
                   data = train, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

cv_model1$results

  intercept     RMSE  Rsquared       MAE     RMSESD RsquaredSD      MAESD
1      TRUE 1.001326 0.4687573 0.7747505 0.06912821 0.06065019 0.05120965
The cross validated RMSE is 1.001. Read it as: on students it has not seen, this model’s predictions are off by about 1 grade points on average.
set.seed(123)
cv_model2 <- train(grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1 + admission_grade,
                   data = train, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

cv_model2$results

  intercept      RMSE  Rsquared       MAE     RMSESD RsquaredSD      MAESD
1      TRUE 0.9966571 0.4739103 0.7712225 0.06950671 0.06109953 0.05054241
RMSE is now 0.997, an improvement of about 0.005 grade points.
set.seed(123)
cv_model3 <- train(grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1 + admission_grade + grade_sem1:admission_grade,
                   data = train, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
RMSE 0.996.
set.seed(123)
cv_model4 <- train(
  grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1 + admission_grade + prev_grade + age + scholarship +
    fees_current + units_sem1 + Gender + Debtor + Displaced,
  data = train, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl
)
RMSE 0.988.
summary(resamples(list(
  model1 = cv_model1,
  model2 = cv_model2,
  model3 = cv_model3,
  model4 = cv_model4
)))$statistics$RMSE

            Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. NA's
model1 0.8545284 0.9746804 0.9945510 1.0013263 1.053863 1.100659    0
model2 0.8526973 0.9660374 0.9902438 0.9966571 1.050061 1.097337    0
model3 0.8588772 0.9626406 0.9881579 0.9956393 1.047992 1.090997    0
model4 0.8482726 0.9454881 0.9843184 0.9875899 1.043208 1.081534    0
Linear regression is widely used largely because its coefficients are easy to interpret. But it relies on several strong assumptions, and those assumptions are violated more often as predictors accumulate. Violations can produce biased estimates, misleading interpretations, and poor predictions.
The model assumes the change in the outcome for a one unit change in a predictor is constant across the whole range of that predictor. Many real relationships are not like that.
Number of units passed in the first semester is a good example.
p1 <- ggplot(train, aes(units_sem1, grade_sem2)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = .2) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "orange") +
  labs(x = "Units passed, first semester", y = "Second semester grade",
       title = "A curved relationship") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p2 <- ggplot(train, aes(units_sem1, grade_sem2)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = .2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Units passed, first semester", y = "Second semester grade",
       title = "A squared term follows it") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, nrow = 1)
A straight line through the left panel would underfit badly. Adding a squared term roughly doubles the variance this predictor accounts for:
c(
  linear    = summary(lm(grade_sem2 ~ units_sem1, data = train))$r.squared,
  quadratic = summary(lm(grade_sem2 ~ units_sem1 + I(units_sem1^2), data = train))$r.squared
)

    linear  quadratic 
0.05954114 0.12027644
Transformations of the predictors, or of the outcome, are often enough to make a relationship approximately linear. The model is still a linear model, because it remains linear in its coefficients.
Heteroskedasticity means the variance of the errors is not constant across levels of the predictors, violating the homoscedasticity assumption.
df1 <- broom::augment(cv_model1$finalModel, data = train)

ggplot(df1, aes(.fitted, .std.resid)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = .3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Predicted values", y = "Standardized residuals",
       title = "Model 1", subtitle = "grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
Look for a funnel shape, where the spread of residuals widens or narrows systematically as predictions get larger. Remedies include transforming the outcome or using robust standard errors.
Heteroskedasticity mainly affects inference, because the standard errors and p values covered in Inference in Linear Regression assume constant variance. The predictions can still be accurate.
Autocorrelation occurs when residuals are correlated with each other, violating the independence assumption. It underestimates standard errors and produces overly optimistic p values. It matters most with a time component or with repeated measures on the same people. Each row here is a different student measured once, so we do not pursue it, though it becomes important with intensive longitudinal data.
The vip() function (Variable Importance Plots) visualizes the relative importance of predictors. It accepts any fitted model object, including lm(), glm(), random forests, and boosted trees.
For linear models, vip() ranks predictors by the absolute value of their t statistics.
vip(cv_model4, num_features = 10, method = "model")
Next: Simple Logistic Regression, which keeps this dataset and changes the outcome from a grade to a category.

title: Simple Linear Regression
text:
Linear regression is usually taught as a statistical model for testing hypotheses.
In this course we will generally treat linear regression as a prediction algorithm.
In this way it learns coefficients from data by minimizing a loss function, uses them to predict new cases, and gets evaluated on data it has never seen.
For now we will skip a discussion of inference in linear regression, but for those who are interested the material can be found here: Inference in Linear Regression.
library(dplyr)   # data manipulation and the pipe
library(ggplot2) # plots
library(naniar)  # missing data visualization
We use the student dropout and academic success data throughout the regression unit. The same dataset returns in Multiple Linear Regression and again in the logistic regression pages, where the outcome changes to a dichotomous variable.
# The file is semicolon separated, which is common in European data, so
# read.csv needs to be told that with sep = ";"
dropout <- read.csv("data/dropout.csv", sep = ";")

# The original column names are long and full of dots once R cleans them up.
# Renaming the handful we use keeps the code below readable.
dropout <- dropout %>%
  rename(
    grade_sem1      = Curricular.units.1st.sem..grade.,
    grade_sem2      = Curricular.units.2nd.sem..grade.,
    admission_grade = Admission.grade,
    age             = Age.at.enrollment,
    scholarship     = Scholarship.holder,
    fees_current    = Tuition.fees.up.to.date
  )

dim(dropout)

[1] 4424   37
Linear regression predicts a continuous outcome from one or more input variables.
Our question: can we predict a student’s second semester grade from their first semester grade?
That is a regression problem because the answer is a number, a grade somewhere on the 0 to 20 scale.
Before modelling anything, look at the data. Start where the Missing Data page told you to start.
# Black would mark missing values, gray observed ones.
# 37 column names are too many to read, so they are hidden.
vis_miss(dropout, warn_large_data = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "37 columns") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())
The plot is entirely gray, so no values are missing.
# Confirm it directly
sum(is.na(dropout))

[1] 0
So the data look clear but let’s dig a little further.
Look at the outcome itself rather than at its missingness.
ggplot(dropout, aes(grade_sem2)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "orange") +
  labs(x = "Second semester grade", y = "Number of students") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
There is a tall spike at zero, then nothing at all until 10.
# How many students sit at exactly zero?
sum(dropout$grade_sem2 == 0)

[1] 870

# What is the lowest grade among everybody else?
min(dropout$grade_sem2[dropout$grade_sem2 > 0])

[1] 10
The zeros are not low grades. Here zero might be a missingness code:
# Of the students with a grade of zero, how many approved zero units?
dropout %>%
  filter(grade_sem2 == 0) %>%
  summarise(
    students          = n(),
    approved_no_units = sum(Curricular.units.2nd.sem..approved. == 0)
  )

  students approved_no_units
1      870               870
Every student with a grade of zero completed no curricular units, so there was no grade to record and the field was filled with a zero instead.
Mixing these two groups would mean fitting one line through students who completed units and students who completed none.
# Keep students who actually completed units in both semesters
completers <- dropout %>%
  filter(grade_sem1 > 0, grade_sem2 > 0)

nrow(completers)

[1] 3512

summary(completers$grade_sem2)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  10.00   11.75   12.67   12.75   13.67   18.57
Start by looking at the relationship.
ggplot(completers, aes(x = grade_sem1, y = grade_sem2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "orange") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(10, 20)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(10, 20)) +
  labs(x = "First semester grade", y = "Second semester grade") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
The orange line is the prediction equation. Written out, it is:
\[
\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x
\]
This equation produces a prediction for any value of \(x\), including values no student in the data had. That is what makes it a prediction algorithm.
Our intercept and slope coefficients from a regression are estimates of parameters learned from the data, not hyperparameters supplied during learning.
The algorithm does not know the right coefficients in advance. It searches for the coefficients that make its predictions as close as possible to the observed outcomes.
To do that it needs a definition of how close a prediction is.
For each student, the residual is what the model got wrong:
\[
e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i
\]
Observed minus predicted. A positive residual means the student did better than predicted, a negative one means worse.
Residuals cannot simply be averaged, because the positives and negatives would cancel. So we square them first, which also makes large misses count for much more than small ones.
Averaging the squared residuals gives the mean squared error:
\[
\operatorname{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
\]
This is the loss function. It is a single number scoring how badly a given pair of coefficients does. Fitting the model means choosing \(b_0\) and \(b_1\) to make that number as small as possible.
This idea stays true for nearly every algorithm in the rest of the course. What changes later is the shape of the prediction equation and sometimes the choice of loss function. The idea of minimizing a loss does not change.
Before searching over many coefficients, score one candidate by hand. Suppose the algorithm tries \(b_0 = 4\) and \(b_1 = 0.7\). Take a student whose first semester grade was 14 and whose second semester grade was 15.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{y} &= b_0 + b_1 x = 4 + 0.7 \times 14 = 13.8 \\
e &= y - \hat{y} = 15 - 13.8 = 1.2 \\
e^2 &= 1.2^2 = 1.44
\end{aligned}
\]
Now do the same thing for five students.
# One candidate pair of coefficients
b0 <- 4
b1 <- 0.7

# Five real students from the data
five <- dropout %>%
  slice(3949, 551, 2860, 2066, 2494) %>%
  select(grade_sem1, grade_sem2) %>%
  mutate(
    y_hat    = b0 + b1 * grade_sem1,  # plug x into the equation
    residual = grade_sem2 - y_hat,    # observed minus predicted
    squared  = residual^2
  )

five

  grade_sem1 grade_sem2 y_hat residual squared
1         11       13.0  11.7      1.3    1.69
2         12       12.0  12.4     -0.4    0.16
3         13       12.5  13.1     -0.6    0.36
4         14       15.0  13.8      1.2    1.44
5         15       12.5  14.5     -2.0    4.00

# Average the squared residuals to get the MSE for this candidate line
mean(five$squared)

[1] 1.53
The student from the formula is the fourth row. In the plot:
For these five students, the MSE of this candidate line is 1.53. Change \(b_0\) or \(b_1\) and the line moves. Every \(\hat{y}\) changes, every residual changes, and the MSE changes with them. Fitting is the search for the line where that number is smallest.
Rather than trusting lm(), try a range of slopes and compute the loss for each:
# Fix the intercept at a sensible value and try many slopes
try_slopes <- seq(0, 1.5, by = 0.01)

# For each candidate slope, compute the mean squared error it produces
loss <- sapply(try_slopes, function(b1) {
  b0   <- mean(completers$grade_sem2) - b1 * mean(completers$grade_sem1)
  pred <- b0 + b1 * completers$grade_sem1
  mean((completers$grade_sem2 - pred)^2)
})

# The slope with the smallest loss
try_slopes[which.min(loss)]

[1] 0.7
ggplot(data.frame(slope = try_slopes, mse = loss), aes(slope, mse)) +
  geom_line(color = "orange", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = try_slopes[which.min(loss)], linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Candidate slope", y = "Mean squared error") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
The curve has one bottom, and the dashed line marks it. That is the slope the algorithm picks. lm() finds this point directly with algebra rather than by trying values, but it is solving the same problem.
fit <- lm(grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1, data = completers)

coef(fit)

(Intercept)  grade_sem1 
  3.8489194   0.6978087
Reading the coefficients as predictions rather than as findings:
Substitute a value to make a prediction by hand:
b <- coef(fit)

# A student who scored 14 in the first semester
b[1] + b[2] * 14

(Intercept) 
   13.61824 

# The same thing, done properly
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(grade_sem1 = 14))

       1 
13.61824
Everything so far used all the data at once. That tells us how well the line fits the students we already have, which is not the question we care about.
The question is how well it predicts students we have never seen.
set.seed(559)

# 70 percent of rows for training, the rest held back
n         <- nrow(completers)
train_idx <- sample(n, size = floor(0.7 * n))

train <- completers[train_idx, ]
test  <- completers[-train_idx, ]

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))

train  test 
 2458  1054
# Estimate the coefficients using the training data only
fit_train <- lm(grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1, data = train)

# Then predict the students the model has never seen
predictions <- predict(fit_train, newdata = test)

head(round(predictions, 2))

    4     6     7    10    15    16 
12.11 13.54 11.79 11.20 11.98 11.81
This is the overarching objective of the course: the coefficients (estimates of the parameters) come from the training data, the evaluation comes from the test data.
We have predictions and we have the truth. Now we need a number summarizing how far apart they are.
actual    <- test$grade_sem2
residuals <- actual - predictions

# MAE: average size of the error, ignoring direction
mae <- mean(abs(residuals))

# RMSE: square, average, then undo the squaring. Large misses count more.
rmse <- sqrt(mean(residuals^2))

c(MAE = mae, RMSE = rmse)

      MAE      RMSE 
0.7752931 1.0063456
Both are in grade points, which is what makes them easy to talk about. An MAE of roughly 0.8 means the typical prediction is off by about eight tenths of a grade point on a 20 point scale.
R squared answers a different question, namely how much of the outcome’s variation the model accounts for:
r2 <- 1 - sum(residuals^2) / sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)
r2

[1] 0.4531134
It is unitless, which makes it easy to compare across problems and easy to over read. For a first lecture, prefer MAE and RMSE, because their units are the units of the thing you are predicting.
A metric on its own is hard to judge. Whether an RMSE of 1.0 is good depends on what you compare it to.
The simplest baseline ignores the predictor entirely and guesses the same value for everybody. The right value to guess is the training mean, because the test set is supposed to be unavailable when you build anything.
baseline_prediction <- mean(train$grade_sem2)

baseline_mae  <- mean(abs(actual - baseline_prediction))
baseline_rmse <- sqrt(mean((actual - baseline_prediction)^2))

rbind(
  model    = c(MAE = mae,          RMSE = rmse),
  baseline = c(MAE = baseline_mae, RMSE = baseline_rmse)
)

               MAE     RMSE
model    0.7752931 1.006346
baseline 1.0834865 1.361074
The model is better than guessing the average, and the table shows by how much.
Nothing about the machinery changes when you add predictors. The equation just gets longer:
\[
\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2
\]
Each coefficient describes how the prediction changes for a one unit increase in its own predictor, holding the others constant.
fit_multi <- lm(grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1 + admission_grade + scholarship,
                data = train)

coef(fit_multi)

    (Intercept)      grade_sem1 admission_grade     scholarship 
     3.03836323      0.67528895      0.00822168      0.16012839
Did it help?
pred_multi <- predict(fit_multi, newdata = test)

c(one_predictor   = rmse,
  three_predictors = sqrt(mean((actual - pred_multi)^2)))

   one_predictor three_predictors 
        1.006346         1.006006
Only slightly. Multiple Linear Regression looks at this in more detail.
Students often assume linear regression can only describe straight lines. It can also describe curves.
Linear regression is linear in its coefficients, not in its predictors. The predictors can be transformed however you like, and the model is still a linear model.
# A squared term is allowed. I() tells R to treat ^2 as arithmetic
# rather than as special formula syntax.
fit_curved <- lm(grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1 + I(grade_sem1^2), data = train)

coef(fit_curved)

    (Intercept)      grade_sem1 I(grade_sem1^2) 
     7.94206832      0.05238366      0.02514251
ggplot(train, aes(grade_sem1, grade_sem2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              aes(color = "straight line")) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE,
              aes(color = "with squared term")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("straight line" = "orange",
                                "with squared term" = "steelblue"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "First semester grade", y = "Second semester grade") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
If the true pattern curves and you insist on a straight line, the model is underfitting: it is too simple to capture what is there, and it will be wrong in a systematic, predictable direction rather than at random.
Here we add 20 predictors of random numbers to a small training sample of 30 students.
set.seed(559)

small_train <- train[1:30, ]
noise_test  <- test

# 20 columns of pure random noise, in both the training and test data
for (j in 1:20) {
  small_train[[paste0("noise", j)]] <- rnorm(nrow(small_train))
  noise_test[[paste0("noise", j)]]  <- rnorm(nrow(noise_test))
}

f <- as.formula(paste("grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1 +",
                      paste0("noise", 1:20, collapse = " + ")))

fit_noise <- lm(f, data = small_train)

# How good does it look on the data it was fit to?
summary(fit_noise)$r.squared

[1] 0.8867479
The training R squared is high. Now score the model on students it has never seen, alongside a model with only grade_sem1 and the baseline:
fit_small <- lm(grade_sem2 ~ grade_sem1, data = small_train)

c(
  with_noise   = sqrt(mean((noise_test$grade_sem2 - predict(fit_noise, noise_test))^2)),
  no_noise     = sqrt(mean((test$grade_sem2      - predict(fit_small, test))^2)),
  baseline     = sqrt(mean((test$grade_sem2      - mean(small_train$grade_sem2))^2))
)

with_noise   no_noise   baseline 
  3.315435   1.008197   1.388660
The model with the noise predictors has a higher test RMSE than the baseline, so it predicts worse than guessing the average. The random columns carry no information, yet the training fit improved. With many predictors and few rows, a model can fit the noise in its training data.
This is overfitting.
# No student in the data has a first semester grade of 2, or of 25
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(grade_sem1 = c(2, 25)))

        1         2 
 5.244537 21.294136
R returns both predictions without a warning, even though 2 is far below anything in the data and 25 is not a possible grade on the 0 to 20 scale.

title: Categorical Feature Engineering
text:
To follow along, load these packages and the dataset we assembled on the Example Data page. If you did not build it yourself, you can download data.RDS and save it in a data folder next to your script.
library(dplyr)       # data manipulation and the pipe
library(tidymodels)  # the recipes package, used for every step below

data <- readRDS("data/data.RDS")
Many models require that the predictors take numeric form. There are exceptionssuch as tree-based models, however, even tree-based methods can benefit from preprocessing categorical features. The following sections will discuss a few of the more common approaches to engineer categorical features.
Sometimes features will contain levels that have very few observations. For example, take a look at the work status variable wrkstat. There are 8 unique levels and some have relatively few observations. For example, With A Job, But Not At Work Because Of Temporary Illness, Vacation, Strike.
# count() tallies how many rows fall into each level of wrkstat and puts the
# tally in a column called n. arrange(n) then sorts by that column, smallest
# first, which brings the rare levels we care about to the top.
count(data, wrkstat) %>% arrange(n)

# A tibble: 9 × 2
  wrkstat                                                                      n
  <fct>                                                                    <int>
1 <NA>                                                                        12
2 With A Job, But Not At Work Because Of Temporary Illness, Vacation, Str…    75
3 In School                                                                  124
4 Other                                                                      130
5 Unemployed, Laid Off, Looking For Work                                     221
6 Keeping House                                                              329
7 Working Part Time                                                          398
8 Retired                                                                    874
9 Working Full Time                                                         1823
Sometimes we can benefit from collapsing, or “lumping” these into a lesser number of categories. In the above examples, we may want to collapse all levels that are observed in less than 5% of the training sample into an Other category. We can use step_other() to do so.
# Write the recipe. step_other() does the lumping.
#   wrkstat          the column to lump, though you can name several
#   threshold = 0.05 any level holding less than 5 percent of the rows
#                    gets collapsed
#   other = "Other"  what to call the new combined level
lumping <- recipe(happy ~ ., data = data) %>%
  step_other(wrkstat, threshold = 0.05,
             other = "Other")

# prep() works out which levels actually fall below the threshold, and bake()
# applies that decision and hands back the changed data. You will see this
# pair again in the Workflow section at the end of the unit.
apply_2_training <- prep(lumping, training = data) %>%
  bake(data)

# Count wrkstat again and compare against the table above. The rare levels
# have been folded into a single Other category.
count(apply_2_training, wrkstat) %>% arrange(n)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  wrkstat                                    n
  <fct>                                  <int>
1 <NA>                                      12
2 Unemployed, Laid Off, Looking For Work   221
3 Keeping House                            329
4 Other                                    329
5 Working Part Time                        398
6 Retired                                  874
7 Working Full Time                       1823
As mentioned previously many models require that all features be numeric. Consequently, we need to intelligently transform any categorical variables into numeric representations so that these algorithms will work.
There are many ways to recode categorical variables as numeric (e.g., one-hot, ordinal, binary, sum, and Helmert).
One-hot encoding is a common method for converting categorical variables into a numerical format that machine learning algorithms can work with. Instead of assigning arbitrary numbers to categories (which could incorrectly imply an order), one-hot encoding creates a new binary (0/1) column for each category level. For a given observation, the column corresponding to its category is set to 1, and all others are set to 0.
However, this creates perfect collinearity which causes problems with some predictive modeling algorithms (e.g., ordinary linear regression and neural networks). Alternatively, we can create a full-rank encoding by dropping one of the levels (level blue has been dropped). This is referred to as dummy coding.
Below is an example of one-hot encoding the predictors in our model.
# step_dummy() turns categorical columns into numeric indicator columns.
#   all_factor_predictors() selects every categorical predictor at once, so
#                           you do not have to name them
#   one_hot = TRUE          make one column per level, as in the first image
#   one_hot = FALSE         drop one level to act as the reference category,
#                           which is the dummy coding in the second image and
#                           what regression models normally want
recipe(happy ~ ., data = data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_factor_predictors(), one_hot = TRUE)
Printing the recipe only shows the plan. It tells you a dummy step exists, but not how many columns it will create, because that is not known until the recipe is prepped and it sees how many levels each variable has.

title: Feature Filtering
text:
To follow along, load these packages and the dataset we assembled on the Example Data page. If you did not build it yourself, you can download data.RDS and save it in a data folder next to your script.
library(dplyr)  # data manipulation and the pipe
library(caret)  # nearZeroVar(), used below to flag low variance features

data <- readRDS("data/data.RDS")
Feature filtering is a feature selection technique in machine learning where features are evaluated prior to the model fitting based on statistical or heuristic criteria. Features are then kept or discarded based on those criteria.
It is called filtering because it is a preprocessing step, part of a feature engineering pipeline, done before we actually train the model.
Typically, the goals of feature filtering are:
In practice, one of the filtering tasks we will typically conduct involves weeding out low variance features.
Zero and near-zero variance variables are low-hanging fruit to eliminate.
Zero and near-zero variance variables typically offer little to no information for model building. Furthermore, resampling (data-splitting) further complicates this picture because a given fold or sample may only contain a single value if the variable itself only contains a few unique values.
Boehmke and Greenwell (2019) suggest the following rule-of-thumb for removing low-variance features:
Remove a variable if:
We can use the caret (Kuhn and Max 2008) package in R to look at these different metrics for our example data.
# nearZeroVar() checks every column against the two rules above.
#   saveMetrics = TRUE returns the diagnostics for every variable. Without it
#   you get back only the column numbers of the ones it would drop, which is
#   useful for code but useless for understanding what is going on.
caret::nearZeroVar(data, saveMetrics = TRUE) %>%

  # the variable names arrive as row names rather than as a real column,
  # which makes them awkward to read, so this moves them into a column
  tibble::rownames_to_column()

   rowname freqRatio percentUnique zeroVar   nzv
1    happy  2.696721    0.07526342   FALSE FALSE
2      age  1.071429    1.80632213   FALSE FALSE
3      sex  1.213766    0.05017561   FALSE FALSE
4     race  3.013580    0.07526342   FALSE FALSE
5     educ  1.141657    0.52684395   FALSE FALSE
6   income 14.668421    0.30105369   FALSE FALSE
7   childs  1.273821    0.22579027   FALSE FALSE
8  wrkstat  2.085812    0.20070246   FALSE FALSE
9  marital  1.243628    0.12543904   FALSE FALSE
10    born  5.458401    0.05017561   FALSE FALSE
11 partyid  1.467164    0.20070246   FALSE FALSE
12  adults  1.075205    0.15052684   FALSE FALSE
13  earnrs  1.419145    0.10035123   FALSE FALSE
Four columns come back. The two that matter are the ones from the rule of thumb above.
In a real pipeline you would not run this by hand. You would add step_nzv() to a recipe and let it happen inside the resampling, for the reasons the Overview gave. Running it here is just so you can see what the decision is based on.

title: Example Data
text:
To demonstrate feature engineering we will use some example data from the The General Social Survey (GSS).
GSS is a long-running, nationally representative survey of adults in the United States that has been conducted almost every two years since 1972 by the National Opinion Research Center (NORC) at the University of Chicago. The GSS data is often used to measure American’s attitudes, behaviors, and beliefs on a wide range of topics, such as politics, religion, crime, race relations, family, work, and technology.
There are two ways to access the GSS data. One is using the GSS Data Explorer. Another option is using the gssr (Healy 2023) R package. Here we will use the gssr (Healy 2023) package to download some example data.
Once it is installed, load these two packages to follow along.
library(gssr)   # downloading the GSS data
library(dplyr)  # data manipulation and the pipe
We will start by choosing happy as our target variable. This comes from Question 157 of the 2024 GSS where respondents were asked:
Responses were coded such that 1 indicates “very happy”, 2 indicates “pretty happy”, and 3 indicates “not too happy”, while NA indicates “don’t know.”
We can also identify a bunch of features we think predict self-reported happiness and save our final dataset.
# Downloads the full 2024 GSS. This is a big file, so it takes a moment.
# The result is a data frame with one row per respondent.
gss24 <- gss_get_yr(2024)

# The variable we want to predict. Storing it in an object rather than
# typing "happy" everywhere means we only have to change it in one place.
target <- "happy"

features <- c(
  "age",     # age of participant
  "sex",     # sex of participant
  "race",    # race of participant
  "educ",    # highest education completed by participant
  "income",  # income of participant
  "childs",  # number of children participant has
  "wrkstat", # work force status
  "marital", # marital status
  "born",    # whether or not participant was born in USA
  "partyid", # political party of participant
  "adults",  # num of fam members 18 or older
  "earnrs"   # number of earners in family  
)

# Square brackets subset a data frame as [rows, columns]. Leaving the rows
# slot empty means "keep every row". The columns slot keeps only our target
# and our features, so we go from around a thousand columns down to 13.
data <- gss24[, c(target, features)]

# table() counts how many times each value appears. useNA = "always" forces
# it to show the count of missing values too, which it would otherwise hide.
# Look at that NA column, because missing data is the subject of the next page.
table(data$happy, useNA = "always")


   1    2    3 <NA> 
 797 2303  854   32
Next, let’s clean up data a bit, discarding some of the labels and missing value information we don’t need. The data in gss24 retains the labeling structure provided by the GSS. Variables are stored numerically with labels attached to them. Often, when using the data in R, it will be convenient to convert the categorical variables we are interested in to character or factor type instead.
Here we can use code from the gssr package introduction to simplify this recoding. The only thing we need to do is define the categorical variables in our data.
# Two lists of column names. c() just glues values together into a vector.
# We write these out once so the code below can refer to a whole group of
# columns by name instead of repeating the same operation seven times.
cat_vars <- c("sex","race", "educ", "wrkstat", "marital", "born", "partyid")
cont_vars <- c("happy", "age", "income", "childs", "adults", "earnrs")

# Tidies up label text. It splits a label on spaces, uppercases the first
# letter of each word, lowercases the rest when strict = TRUE, then pastes the
# words back together. This is what turns "NEVER MARRIED" into "Never Married".
capwords <- function(x, strict = FALSE) {
    cap <- function(x) paste(toupper(substring(x, 1, 1)),
                  {x <- substring(x, 2); if(strict) tolower(x) else x},
                             sep = "", collapse = " " )
    sapply(strsplit(x, split = " "), cap, USE.NAMES = !is.null(names(x)))
}

# mutate() applies each of the four steps below to the columns named in it.
# across() is what lets one line act on a whole set of columns at once.
data <- data |>
  mutate(

    # The GSS does not leave unanswered questions blank. It fills them with
    # special codes for things like "Don't know" and "No answer". zap_missing
    # turns every one of those codes into a plain NA so the rest of R treats
    # them consistently. This has to run first. If we converted the columns
    # below before clearing these codes, the codes would survive as if they
    # were real answers.
    across(everything(), haven::zap_missing),

    # The continuous variables arrive carrying the GSS labelling structure.
    # as.numeric strips that off and leaves plain numbers we can do arithmetic
    # on, such as taking a mean.
    across(all_of(cont_vars), as.numeric),

    # The categorical variables get the opposite treatment. as_factor converts
    # the stored numeric codes into a factor using the labels the GSS ships
    # with the data, so a stored 1 becomes its written category instead.
    across(all_of(cat_vars), forcats::as_factor),

    # Those labels arrive in all capitals. fct_relabel runs every level of the
    # factor through capwords to clean them up. The \(x) is shorthand for
    # function(x), which we need here only because we want to pass capwords its
    # strict = TRUE argument.
    across(all_of(cat_vars), \(x) forcats::fct_relabel(x, capwords, strict = TRUE))
  )

title: A Complete Pipeline
text:
We now have all the pieces. This page runs them end to end, once, on the Ames housing data.
To follow along, load these six packages.
library(rsample)      # splitting
library(recipes)      # preprocessing
library(caret)        # fitting and cross validation
library(AmesHousing)  # the example data
library(dplyr)        # the pipe used in the recipe below
library(glmnet)       # the second model we fit, in step 5
The pipeline is six steps:
Before we do anything else, we set aside the data we are not allowed to look at.
# make_ames() builds the Ames housing data frame for us. It comes from the
# AmesHousing package we loaded above, so there is no file to download.
ames <- make_ames()

# dim() reports the number of rows and then the number of columns
dim(ames)

[1] 2930   81
# The split is random, so we fix R's random number generator first. Without
# this line you get a different split every time you run the file, and none
# of your numbers reproduce. The number 559 is arbitrary. Any number works,
# as long as you use the same one each time.
set.seed(559)

# initial_split() does not hand back data. It hands back a set of
# instructions recording which rows belong on which side.
#   prop   = 0.7           put 70 percent of the rows in the training set
#   strata = "Sale_Price"  split within price bands, so both sides end up
#                          with a similar mix of cheap and expensive houses
split <- initial_split(ames, prop = 0.7, strata = "Sale_Price")

# training() and testing() are what actually give you the two data frames
ames_train <- training(split)
ames_test  <- testing(split)

# Check that the sizes came out roughly where we expected
c(train = nrow(ames_train), test = nrow(ames_test))

train  test 
 2049   881
From this point until step 6, ames_test does not appear anywhere. That single sentence is the whole discipline of this page.
Most data need work before modelling. A recipe is a written list of those steps that is learned from the training data and then applied elsewhere.
# recipe() takes a formula and some data.
#   Sale_Price ~ ...  the thing on the left of the ~ is what we predict,
#                     everything on the right is what we predict it from
#   data = ames_train only the training data, never the full dataset
#
# The %>% is the pipe. It takes whatever is on its left and feeds it into
# the function on its right, so each step_ below is added to the growing
# recipe one after another.
rec <- recipe(Sale_Price ~ Gr_Liv_Area + Year_Built + Neighborhood,
              data = ames_train) %>%
  step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), threshold = 0.05) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors())

# Printing the recipe shows the plan. Notice it has not touched any data yet.
rec
The helpers inside the parentheses are how you say “all the columns of this kind” without typing their names. all_nominal_predictors() means every categorical predictor, all_numeric_predictors() means every numeric one. This matters because step_dummy creates new columns, so you cannot know all the column names in advance anyway.
A recipe on its own is only a plan. Two more functions make it real, and you will meet both again throughout the course.
You do not normally call these yourself, because train() does it for you in step 4. We do it here once just so you can see the output.
# Learn the numbers from the training data
rec_prepped <- prep(rec)

# Apply them. new_data = NULL is the way to say "give me back the training
# data you already prepped" rather than handing it some new dataset.
baked <- bake(rec_prepped, new_data = NULL)

# The original three predictors have become many more columns, because
# step_dummy turned each neighborhood into its own 0/1 indicator
dim(baked)

[1] 2049   10

head(names(baked), 10)

 [1] "Gr_Liv_Area"                     "Year_Built"                     
 [3] "Sale_Price"                      "Neighborhood_College_Creek"     
 [5] "Neighborhood_Old_Town"           "Neighborhood_Edwards"           
 [7] "Neighborhood_Somerset"           "Neighborhood_Northridge_Heights"
 [9] "Neighborhood_Gilbert"            "Neighborhood_other"
We still need a way to compare models without touching the test set. That is what cross validation is for, and trainControl() is where you describe it.
# This object is just a set of instructions. It does not run anything yet.
#   method = "cv"  use k fold cross validation
#   number = 10    use 10 folds
#
# In words: chop the training data into 10 pieces, hold each piece out in
# turn, fit on the other 9, and score on the piece that was held out.
cv <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)
Notice we have now written down three things and fit nothing. A split, a recipe, and a resampling plan. Step 4 is where they all get used at once.
Passing the recipe to train() rather than a formula means the recipe is re-learned inside every fold, on that fold’s training portion only. That is what keeps the leakage protection honest during cross validation.
# train() refits inside every fold, and the folds are chosen randomly, so we
# set the seed again to make the whole thing reproducible
set.seed(559)

fit_lm <- train(
  rec,                    # the recipe from step 2, not a formula
  data      = ames_train, # training data only
  method    = "lm",       # ordinary linear regression
  trControl = cv,         # the resampling plan from step 3
  metric    = "RMSE"      # the number used to judge the model
)

fit_lm$results

  intercept     RMSE  Rsquared      MAE   RMSESD RsquaredSD    MAESD
1      TRUE 43472.56 0.7036137 29168.58 5757.255 0.05438564 1833.813
That one row is the summary of ten separate model fits.
The no free lunch theorem from Important Terms and Distinctions said we cannot know in advance which method wins. So we try more than one and compare them on the same folds.
Here is a lasso model, which has a hyperparameter to tune. Lasso is a linear regression that pays a penalty for large coefficients, and lambda sets how steep that penalty is. What it is really doing is the subject of the regression unit. The only thing that matters here is that it has a knob on it, and that cross validation is what turns the knob.
tuneGrid lists the values to try. Setting alpha = 1 is what makes this lasso rather than one of the other penalized models glmnet can fit.
set.seed(559)

fit_lasso <- train(
  rec,
  data      = ames_train,
  method    = "glmnet",   # the package that fits penalized regressions
  trControl = cv,         # the same resampling plan as before
  metric    = "RMSE",

  # expand.grid() builds a table of every combination of the values you give
  # it. Here alpha is fixed at 1 and lambda takes five values, so we get five
  # candidate settings, and caret scores each one by cross validation.
  tuneGrid  = expand.grid(alpha = 1, lambda = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000))
)

# Pull out just the columns worth looking at
fit_lasso$results[, c("lambda", "RMSE", "Rsquared", "MAE")]

  lambda     RMSE  Rsquared      MAE
1      1 43469.88 0.7036503 29132.84
2     10 43469.88 0.7036503 29132.84
3    100 43469.88 0.7036503 29132.84
4   1000 43516.87 0.7033676 29019.89
5  10000 46375.63 0.6917134 30408.76
Each row is one value of lambda, scored by cross validation. Notice the shape of that column. Small penalties barely move the model, so those rows are nearly identical. Once the penalty gets large enough it starts squashing coefficients that were doing useful work, and the error climbs.
This is the bias variance tradeoff showing up as a column of numbers. Too little penalty and the model chases noise. Too much and it cannot follow the signal.
train() keeps the best row for you:
# bestTune reports the setting that won, and it is the one train() will use
# when you later call predict()
fit_lasso$bestTune

  alpha lambda
3     1    100
Because both models used the same seed and the same resampling plan, they were scored on exactly the same 10 folds. That is what makes the comparison fair. If the folds differed, you could not tell whether a difference came from the model or from an easier set of folds.
# resamples() collects the fold by fold results of several fitted models so
# they can be compared side by side
results <- resamples(list(linear = fit_lm, lasso = fit_lasso))

# The RMSE distribution across folds for each model
summary(results)$statistics$RMSE

           Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. NA's
linear 36530.25 39682.47 41511.62 43472.56 46361.51 53040.55    0
lasso  36524.43 39658.83 41508.00 43469.88 46366.21 53023.37    0
The two are essentially tied. That is a real result rather than a broken comparison. We gave the model three predictors and roughly two thousand training rows, so there is nothing here for a penalty to clean up, and lasso settles on very nearly the ordinary linear fit. Penalties start to matter when there are many predictors relative to rows, which is the situation the regression unit picks up.
Pick the winner, then look at the test data for the first and only time. The two candidates tied, so we keep the simpler one.
# Choosing the model is a decision, and it was made using the cross
# validated numbers above, not the test set
final_model <- fit_lm

# predict() applies the whole pipeline to new data. The recipe travels with
# the model, so the test rows get lumped, normalized, and dummy coded using
# the values learned from the training data. You do not redo any of it.
test_predictions <- predict(final_model, ames_test)

# postResample() compares predictions against the truth and returns all
# three regression metrics at once
postResample(pred = test_predictions, obs = ames_test$Sale_Price)

        RMSE     Rsquared          MAE 
4.196908e+04 7.232742e-01 2.792871e+04
That is the number you report. It is an estimate of how the model will perform on houses nobody has seen.
It is worth comparing it to the cross validated RMSE from step 4. They will not match exactly, and neither one is wrong. The cross validated number was an estimate made from the training data. This one is measured on data the model has genuinely never seen. If the test number were dramatically worse, that would be a signal that something in the pipeline had been fit too closely to the training data.
Every pipeline in this course has this shape, whatever the model:
# 1. split
split <- initial_split(data, prop = 0.7, strata = "outcome")
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

# 2. recipe
rec <- recipe(outcome ~ ., data = train) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

# 3. resampling
cv <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

# 4 and 5. fit, tune, compare
fit <- train(rec, data = train, method = "lm",
             trControl = cv, metric = "RMSE")

# 6. once
postResample(predict(fit, test), test$outcome)
From here the course mostly changes one thing at a time. The regression unit changes what goes in method. The feature engineering unit changes what goes in the recipe. The tree unit changes both. The pipeline stays the same.

title: Splitting and Resampling in R
text:
The Data Splitting page explained why we hold data back. This page does it in R.
To follow along, load these three packages first. All of them came with the course setup, so you should not need to install anything.
library(rsample)      # splitting and resampling
library(caret)        # fitting and cross validation
library(AmesHousing)  # the example data
Everything on this page and the two that follow uses the Ames housing data, which the regression unit also uses.
ames <- make_ames()

dim(ames)

[1] 2930   81

summary(ames$Sale_Price)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  12789  129500  160000  180796  213500  755000
Prices run from about $13,000 to $755,000 with a median near $160,000, and the mean sits above the median because a handful of expensive houses pull the distribution to the right. That skew matters later, both for stratified splitting and for the difference between RMSE and MAE.
The rsample package handles splitting. Three functions do almost all of the work:
set.seed(559)

split <- initial_split(ames, prop = 0.7)

ames_train <- training(split)
ames_test  <- testing(split)

c(train = nrow(ames_train), test = nrow(ames_test))

train  test 
 2051   879
Two things to notice.
A plain random split can get unlucky. If expensive houses land mostly in one half, the two halves are not comparable.
strata fixes this by splitting within groups of the outcome and then combining.
set.seed(559)

split <- initial_split(ames, prop = 0.7, strata = "Sale_Price")

ames_train <- training(split)
ames_test  <- testing(split)

c(train_mean = mean(ames_train$Sale_Price),
  test_mean  = mean(ames_test$Sale_Price))

train_mean  test_mean 
  180992.6   180338.9
The two means now sit close together by construction rather than by luck.
Stratifying matters most when:
The previous page described k fold cross validation in six steps. In caret those six steps are one function call.
trainControl() describes how to resample. train() does the fitting.
cv <- trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 10
)
That says: split the training data into 10 folds, hold each fold out in turn, fit on the other 9, and score on the held out fold.
Now fit a model using it.
set.seed(559)

fit_cv <- train(
  Sale_Price ~ Gr_Liv_Area,
  data      = ames_train,
  method    = "lm",
  trControl = cv
)

fit_cv

Linear Regression 

2049 samples
   1 predictor

No pre-processing
Resampling: Cross-Validated (10 fold) 
Summary of sample sizes: 1845, 1843, 1845, 1844, 1844, 1843, ... 
Resampling results:

  RMSE      Rsquared   MAE     
  56673.75  0.4986834  38454.31

Tuning parameter 'intercept' was held constant at a value of TRUE
The reported RMSE is the average across the 10 folds, not a single number from a single split. That is the whole point: one holdout split gives an unstable estimate, and averaging ten of them gives a steadier one.
It is worth being explicit, because train() hides a lot:
Note what did not happen. The test set was never touched. It is still sitting untouched in ames_test, which is exactly where it should stay until the very end.
method accepts more than "cv":
"repeatedcv" is useful when your dataset is small enough that a single set of folds is itself noisy:
cv_rep <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 10, repeats = 5)
Next: Evaluating Model Performance, which explains what that RMSE number actually measures.

title: Data Splitting
text:
Data splitting (e.g., dividing data into training, validation, and test samples) is crucial because it protects us from fooling ourselves about how well a model actually performs.
In our discussion of the training and validation samples we introduce the idea of parameters and hyperparameters. The distinction between these terms can often can trip people up, so it’s worth explaining the difference.
When we split data, each portion plays a distinct role:
So, what does all this data splitting mean for us in practice? Let’s take a look at one of the more popular data-splitting methods used in practice: K-Folds Cross-Validation
When talking about data-splitting we discussed training, validation and test sets. For a moment, let’s take a closer look at the training and validation sets to get a clear idea of what is happening.
Let’s split our available data into two parts:
This method is simple and useful. It gives us an early warning if our model is overfitting. However, relying on a single holdout split comes with a big drawback: the result can be very unstable.
This idea motivates a better solution: cross-validation, where we avoid putting all our faith in just one split of the data. Instead, we systematically rotate through multiple splits, averaging the results to get a more stable and reliable estimate of model performance.
One idea is to break up our data into a number of training and validation sets as the image below shows. We can then average the performance across the k folds to get a more stable estimate of the model performance.
Sometimes it is helpful to write out the steps of a procedure like this explicitly.
Notice that every splitting procedure above starts by randomly shuffling or sampling the data. Randomness creates a practical problem: if you and I split the same dataset, we get different splits, and different results. Run it twice yourself and you’ll get two answers:
sample(1:10, 3) # randomly draw 3 numbers

[1] 5 6 1

sample(1:10, 3) # run it again... different draw

[1] 10  1  3
R’s random numbers are actually pseudo-random: they come from a sequence determined by a starting point called the seed. If we set the seed ourselves, the “random” results become exactly reproducible:
set.seed(559)
sample(1:10, 3)

[1]  8  4 10

set.seed(559)
sample(1:10, 3) # same seed, same draw

[1]  8  4 10
This is why nearly every machine learning script you’ll see this semester begins with set.seed() before splitting data or fitting models that involve randomness. It doesn’t make the analysis less random in spirit; it makes your random choices repeatable, so your results can be checked by others (including the you of next week, and me when grading).
